{{Short description|none}}
This is a '''glossary of [[representation theory]]''' in [[mathematics]].

The term "module" is often used synonymously for a representation; for the module-theoretic terminology, see also [[glossary of module theory]].

See also [[Glossary of Lie groups and Lie algebras]], [[list of representation theory topics]] and [[:Category:Representation theory]].<!-- this glossary should include all of the topics listed in the last two pages.-->

'''Notations''': We write <math>\mathbb{G}_m = GL_1</math>. Thus, for example, a one-representation (i.e., a character) of a group ''G'' is of the form <math>\chi: G \to \mathbb{G}_m</math>.

{{Compact ToC|short1|sym=yes|x=[[#XYZ|XYZ]]|y=|z=|seealso=yes|refs=yes}}<!--==!$@==-->

==A==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Adams}}
{{defn|1=[[Adams operations]].}}

{{term|1=adjoint}}
{{defn|1=The [[adjoint representation]] of a Lie group ''G'' is the representation given by the adjoint action of ''G'' on the Lie algebra of ''G'' (an adjoint action is obtained, roughly, by differentiating a conjugation action.)}}

{{term|1=admissible}}
{{defn|1=A representation of a real reductive group is called [[admissible representation|admissible]] if (1) a maximal compact subgroup ''K'' acts as unitary operators and (2) each irreducible representation of ''K'' has finite multiplicity.}}

{{term|1=alternating}}
{{defn|1=The [[Symmetric and alternating squares|alternating square]] of a representation ''V'' is a subrepresentation <math>\operatorname{Alt}^2(V)</math> of the second [[tensor power]] <math>V^{\otimes 2}=V\otimes V</math>.}}

{{term|1=Artin}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Emil Artin]].}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Artin's theorem on induced characters]] states that a character on a finite group is a rational linear combination of characters induced from cyclic subgroups.}}
{{defn|no=3|[[Artin representation]] is used in the definition of the [[Artin conductor]].}}

{{term|automorphic}}
{{defn|1=[[automorphic representation]]}}
{{glossary end}}

== B ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Borel–Weil–Bott theorem}}
{{defn|1=Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the [[Borel–Weil–Bott theorem]] realizes an irreducible representation of a [[reductive algebraic group]] as the space of the global sections of a line bundle on a flag variety. (In the positive characteristic case, the construction only produces [[Weyl module]]s, which may not be irreducible.)}}

{{term|branching}}
{{defn|1=[[branching rule]]}}

{{term|1=Brauer}}
{{defn|1=[[Brauer's theorem on induced characters]] states that a character on a finite group is a linear combination with integer coefficients of characters induced from elementary subgroups.}}

{{glossary end}}

==C==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Cartan–Weyl theory}}
{{defn|1=Another name for the [[representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras]].}}

{{term|1=Casimir element}}
{{defn|1=A [[Casimir element]] is a distinguished element of the center of the universal enveloping algebra of a Lie algebra.}}

{{term|1=category of representations}}
{{defn|1=Representations and equivariant maps between them form a [[category of representations]].}}

{{term|1=character}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[character (representation theory)|character]] is a one-dimensional representation.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The character of a finite-dimensional representation π is the function <math>g \mapsto \operatorname{tr} \pi(g)</math>. In other words, it is the composition <math>G \overset{\pi}\to GL(V) \overset{\operatorname{tr}}\to \mathbb{G}_m</math>.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=An [[irreducible character]] (resp. a [[trivial character]]) is the character of an irreducible representation (resp. a trivial representation).}}
{{defn|no=4|1=The [[character group]] of a group ''G'' is the group of all characters on ''G''; namely, <math>\operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{G}_m)</math>.}}
{{defn|no=5|1=The [[character ring]] is the group ring (over the integers) of the character group of ''G''.}}
{{defn|no=6|1=A virtual character is an element of a character ring.}}
{{defn|no=7|1=A [[distributional character]] may be defined for an infinite-dimensional representation.}}
{{defn|no=8|1=An [[infinitesimal character]].}}

{{term|1=Chevalley}}
{{defn|no=1|1=Chevalley}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Chevalley generators]]}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Chevalley group]].}}
{{defn|no=4|1=[[Chevalley's restriction theorem]].}}

{{term|1=class function}}
{{defn|1=A [[class function]] ''f'' on a group ''G'' is a function such that <math>f(g) = f(h g h^{-1})</math>; it is a function on conjugacy classes.}}

{{term|1=cluster algebra}}
{{defn|1=A [[cluster algebra]] is an integral domain with some combinatorial structure on the generators, introduced in an attempt to systematize the notion of a [[dual canonical basis]].}}

{{term|1=coadjoint}}
{{defn|1=A [[coadjoint representation]] is the dual representation of an adjoint representation.}}

{{term|1=complete}}
{{defn|1=“completely reducible" is another term for "semisimple".}}

{{term|1=complex}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[complex representation]] is a representation of ''G'' on a complex vector space. Many authors refer complex representations simply as representations.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[complex-conjugate]] <math>\overline{V}</math> of a complex representation ''V'' is the representation with the same underlying additive group ''V'' with the linear action of ''G'' but with the action of a complex number through complex conjugation.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=A complex representation is self-conjugate if it is isomorphic to its complex conjugate.}}

{{term|1=complementary}}
{{defn|1=A complementary representation to a subrepresentation ''W'' of a representation ''V'' is a representation ''W{{'}}'' such that ''V'' is the direct sum of ''W'' and ''W{{'}}''.}}
{{term|1=cuspidal}}
{{defn|1=[[cuspidal representation]]}}

{{term|1=crystal}}
{{defn|1=[[crystal basis]]}}

{{term|cyclic}}
{{defn|1=A cyclic ''G''-module is a ''G''-module generated by a single vector. For example, an irreducible representation is necessarily cyclic.}}

{{glossary end}}

==D==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Dedekind}}
{{defn|1=[[Dedekind's theorem on linear independence of characters]].}}

{{term|1=defined over}}
{{defn|1=Given a field extension <math>K/F</math>, a representation ''V'' of a group ''G'' over ''K'' is said to be [[field of definition|defined over ''F'']] if <math>V \simeq V_0 \otimes_F K</math> for some representation <math>V_0</math> over ''F'' such that <math>g: V \to V</math> is induced by <math>g: V_0 \to V_0</math>; i.e., <math> g \cdot (v \otimes \lambda) = g v \otimes \lambda</math>. Here, <math>V_0</math> is called an ''F''-form of ''V'' (and is not necessarily unique).}}

{{term|Demazure}}
{{defn|[[Demazure's character formula]]}}

{{term|1=direct sum}}
{{defn|1=The [[direct sum of representations]] ''V'', ''W'' is a representation that is the direct sum <math>V \oplus W</math> of the vector spaces together with the linear group action <math>\pi_{V \oplus W}(g)(v + w) = \pi_V(g)v + \pi_W(g)w</math>.}}

{{term|1=discrete}}
{{defn|1=An irreducible representation of a Lie group ''G'' is said to be in the [[discrete series]] if the matrix coefficients of it are all square integrable. For example, if ''G'' is compact, then every irreducible representation of it is in the discrete series.}}

{{term|1=dominant}}
{{defn|1=The irreducible representations of a simply-connected compact Lie group are indexed by their highest weight. These ''dominant weights'' form the lattice points in an orthant in the weight lattice of the Lie group.}}

{{term|1=dual}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[dual representation]] (or the contragredient representation) of a representation ''V'' is a representation that is the dual vector space <math>V^* = \operatorname{Hom}(V, k)</math> together with the linear group action that preserves the natural pairing <math>V^* \times V \to k</math>}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A [[dual canonical basis]] is a dual of [[Lusztig's canonical basis]].}}

{{glossary end}}

==E==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Eisenstein}}
{{defn|1=[[Eisenstein series]]}}

{{term|1=equivariant}}
{{defn|1=The term “''G''-equivariant” is another term for “''G''-linear”.}}

{{term|1=exterior}}
{{defn|1=An [[exterior power of a representation]] ''V'' is a representation <math>\wedge^n(V)</math> with the group action induced by <math>V^{\otimes n} \to \wedge^n(V)</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

==F==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=faithful}}
{{defn|1=A [[faithful representation]] <math>\pi: G \to GL(V)</math> is a representation such that <math>\pi</math> is [[injective function|injective]] as a function.}}

{{term|1=fiber functor}}
{{defn|1=[[fiber functor]].}}

{{term|1=Frobenius reciprocity}}
{{defn|1=The [[Frobenius reciprocity]] states that for each representation <math>\sigma</math> of ''H'' and representation <math>\pi</math> of ''G'' there is a bijection
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}_G(\pi, \operatorname{Ind}_H^G \sigma) = \operatorname{Hom}_H(\pi|_H, \sigma)</math>
that is natural in the sense that <math>\operatorname{Ind}_H^G</math> is the right [[adjoint functor]] to the restriction functor <math>\pi \mapsto \pi|_H</math>.}}

{{term|1=fundamental}}
{{defn|1=[[Fundamental representation]]: For the irreducible representations of a simply-connected [[compact Lie group]] there exists a set of ''fundamental weights'', indexed by the vertices of the [[Dynkin diagram]] of G, such that ''dominant weights'' are simply non-negative integer linear combinations of the fundamental weights.

The corresponding irreducible representations are the ''fundamental representations'' of the Lie group. In particular, from the expansion of a dominant weight in terms of the fundamental weights, one can take a corresponding [[tensor product]] of the fundamental representations and extract one copy of the irreducible representation corresponding to that dominant weight.

In the case of the [[special unitary group]] ''SU''(''n''), the ''n'' &minus; 1 fundamental representations are the wedge products

:<math>Alt^k\ {\mathbb C}^n</math>

consisting of [[alternating tensor]]s, for k=1,2,...,n-1.}}

{{glossary end}}

==G==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=''G''-linear}}
{{defn|1=A [[equivariant map|''G''-linear map]] <math>f: V \to W</math> between representations is a linear transformation that commutes with the ''G''-actions; i.e., <math>f \circ \pi_V(g) = \pi_W(g) \circ f</math> for every ''g'' in ''G''.}}

{{term|1=''G''-module}}
{{defn|1=Another name for a representation. It allows for the module-theoretic terminology: e.g., trivial ''G''-module, ''G''-submodules, etc.}}

{{term|1=''G''-equivariant vector bundle}}
{{defn|1=A [[equivariant vector bundle|''G''-equivariant vector bundle]] is a vector bundle <math>p: E \to X</math> on a ''G''-space ''X'' together with a ''G''-action on ''E'' (say right) such that <math>g: p^{-1}(x) \to p^{-1}(xg)</math> is a well-defined linear map.}}

{{term|1=Galois}}
{{defn|1=[[Galois representation]].}}

{{term|1=good}}
{{defn|1=A [[good filtration]] of a representation of a [[reductive group]] ''G'' is a filtration such that the quotients are isomorphic to <math>H^0(\lambda) = \Gamma(G/B, L_\lambda)</math> where <math>L_\lambda</math> are the line bundles on the flag variety <math>G/B</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

==H==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Harish-Chandra}}
{{defn|no=1|1= [[Harish-Chandra]] (11 October 1923 – 16 October 1983), an Indian American mathematician.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[Harish-Chandra Plancherel theorem]].}}

{{term|1=highest weight}}
{{defn|no=1|1=Given a complex semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> and a choice of a [[positive Weyl chamber]], the [[highest weight]] of a representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is the weight of an <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>-weight vector ''v'' such that <math>E_{\alpha} v = 0</math> for every positive root <math>\alpha</math> (''v'' is called the highest weight vector).}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[theorem of the highest weight]] states (1) two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> are isomorphic if and only if they have the same highest weight and (2) for each dominant integral <math>\lambda \in \mathfrak{h}^*</math>, there is a finite-dimensional irreducible representation having <math>\lambda</math> as its highest weight.}}

{{term|1=Hom}}
{{defn|The [[Hom representation]] <math>\operatorname{Hom}(V, W)</math> of representations ''V'', ''W'' is a representation with the group action obtained by the vector space identification <math>\operatorname{Hom}(V, W) = V^* \otimes W</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

==I==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=indecomposable}}
{{defn|1=An [[indecomposable representation]] is a representation that is not a direct sum of at least two proper subrepresebtations.}}

{{term|1=induction}}
{{defn|no=1|Given a representation <math>(\sigma, W)</math> of a subgroup ''H'' of a group ''G'', the [[induced representation]]
:<math>\operatorname{Ind}_H^G(\sigma) = \{ f: G \to W | f(hg) = \sigma(h) f(g) \}</math>
is a representation of ''G'' that is induced on the ''H''-linear functions <math>f: G \to W</math>; cf. [[#Frobenius reciprocity]].}}
{{defn|no=2|Depending on applications, it is common to impose further conditions on the functions <math>f: G \to W</math>; for example, if the functions are required to be compactly supported, then the resulting induction is called the [[compact induction]].}}

{{term|1=infinitesimally}}
{{defn|1=Two admissible representations of a real reductive group are said to be [[infinitesimally equivalent]] if their associated Lie algebra representations on the space of ''K''-finite vectors are isomorphic.}}

{{term|1=integrable}}
{{defn|1=A representation of a [[Kac–Moody algebra]] is said to be [[integrable module|integrable]] if (1) it is a sum of weight spaces and (2) Chevalley generators <math>e_i, f_i</math> are [[locally nilpotent endomorphism|locally nilpotent]].}}

{{term|1=intertwining}}
{{defn|1=The term "[[intertwining operator]]" is an old name for a ''G''-linear map between representations.}}

{{term|1=involution}}
{{defn|1=An [[involution representation]] is a representation of a [[C*-algebra]] on a Hilbert space that preserves involution.}}

{{term|1=irreducible}}
{{defn|1=An [[irreducible representation]] is a representation whose only subrepresentations are zero and itself. The term "irreducible" is synonymous with "simple".}}

{{term|1=isomorphism}}
{{defn|1=An isomorphism between representations of a group ''G'' is an invertible ''G''-linear map between the representations.}}

{{term|1=isotypic}}
{{defn|no=1|1=Given a representation ''V'' and a simple representation ''W'' (subrepresebtation or otherwise), the [[isotypic component]] of ''V'' of type ''W'' is the direct sum of all subrepresentations of ''V'' that are isomorphic to ''W''. For example, let ''A'' be a ring and ''G'' a group acting on it as automorphisms. If ''A'' is [[semisimple representation|semisimple]] as a ''G''-module, then the [[ring of invariants]] <math>A^G</math> is the isotypic component of ''A'' of trivial type.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[isotypic decomposition]] of a semisimple representation is the decomposition into the isotypic components.}}
{{glossary end}}

==J==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=Jacquet}}
{{defn|1=[[Jacquet functor]]}}

{{glossary end}}

==K==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=Kac}}
{{defn|1=The [[Kac character formula]]}}

{{term|1=K-finite}}
{{defn|1=A vector ''v'' in a representation space of a group ''K'' is said to be ''K''-finite if <math>K \cdot v</math> spans a finite-dimensional vector space.}}

{{term|1=Kirillov}}
{{defn|1=The [[Kirillov character formula]]}}

{{glossary end}}

==L==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=lattice}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[root lattice]] is the free abelian group generated by the roots.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[weight lattice]] is the group of all linear functionals <math>\chi \in \mathfrak{h}^*</math> on a Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> that are integral: <math>\chi(H_{\alpha})</math> is an integer for every root <math>\alpha</math>.}}

{{term|Littlemann}}
{{defn|1=[[Littelmann path model]]}}

{{glossary end}}

==M==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Maschke's theorem}}
{{defn|1=[[Maschke's theorem]] states that a finite-dimensional representation over a field ''F'' of a finite group ''G'' is a [[semisimple representation]] if the characteristic of ''F'' does not divide the order of ''G''.}}

{{term|1=Mackey theory}}
{{defn|1=The [[Mackey theory]] may be thought of a tool to answer the question: given a representation ''W'' of a subgroup ''H'' of a group ''G'', when is the induced representation <math>\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W</math> an irreducible representation of ''G''?<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/~nd332/Mackey.pdf |title=Induction and Mackey Theory |access-date=2017-11-23 |archive-date=2017-12-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201032703/https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/~nd332/Mackey.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>}}

{{term|1=Maass–Selberg}}
{{defn|1=[[Maass–Selberg relations]].}}

{{term|1=matrix coefficient}}
{{defn|1=A [[matrix coefficient]] of a representation <math>\pi: G \to GL(V)</math> is a linear combination of functions on ''G'' of the form <math>g \mapsto \langle \pi(g) v, \alpha \rangle</math> for ''v'' in ''V'' and <math>\alpha</math> in the dual space <math>V^*</math>. Note the notion makes sense for any group: if ''G'' is a topological group and <math>\pi</math> is continuous, then a matrix matrix coefficient would be a continuous function on ''G''. If ''G'' and <math>\pi</math> are algebraic, it would be a [[regular function]] on ''G''.}}

{{term|modular}}
{{defn|1=The [[modular representation theory]].}}

{{term|Molien}}
{{defn|1=Given a finite-dimensional complex representation ''V'' of a finite group ''G'', [[Molien's theorem]] says that the series <math>\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \dim (\mathbb{C}[V]^G)_n t^n</math>, where <math>(\mathbb{C}[V]^G)_n</math> denotes the space of <math>G</math>-invariant homogeneous polynomials on ''V'' of degree ''n'', coincides with <math>(\# G)^{-1} \sum_{g \in G} \det(1 - t g |V)^{-1}</math>. The theorem is also valid for a reductive group by replacing <math>(\# G)^{-1} \sum_{g \in G}</math> by integration over a maximal compact subgroup.<!-- the extension due to H. Weyl? -->}}

{{glossary end}}

==O==
{{glossary}}

{{term|Oscillator}}
{{defn|1=[[Oscillator representation]]}}

{{term|orbit}}
{{defn|[[orbit method]], an approach to representation theory that uses tools from symplectic geometry}}

{{glossary end}}

==P==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Peter–Weyl}}
{{defn|1=The [[Peter–Weyl theorem]] states that the linear span of the [[matrix coefficient]]s on a compact group ''G'' is dense in <math>L^2(G)</math>.}}

{{term|1=permutation}}
{{defn|1=Given a group ''G'', a ''G''-set ''X'' and ''V'' the vector space of functions from ''X'' to a fixed field, a [[permutation representation]] <math>\pi</math> of ''G'' on ''V'' is a representation given by the induced action of ''G'' on ''V''; i.e., <math>(\pi(g)v)(x) = v(g^{-1} x)</math>. For example, if ''X'' is a finite set and ''V'' is viewed as a vector space with a basis parameteized by ''X'', then the symmetric group <math>G = \operatorname{Sym}(X)</math> permutates the elements of the basis and its linear extension is precisely the permutation representation.}}

{{term|Plancherel}}
{{defn|1=[[Plancherel formula]]}}

{{term|positive-energy representation}}
{{defn|1=[[positive-energy representation]].}}

{{term|primitive}}
{{defn|1=The term "primitive element" (or a vector) is an old term for a Borel-weight vector.}}

{{term|1=projective}}
{{defn|1=A [[projective representation]] of a group ''G'' is a group homomorphism <math>\pi: G \to PGL(V) = GL(V)/\mathbb{G}_m</math>. Since <math>PGL(V) = \operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{P}(V))</math>, a projective representation is precisely a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] of ''G'' on <math>\mathbb{P}(V)</math> as automorphisms.}}

{{term|1=proper}}
{{defn|1=A proper subrepresentation of a representation ''V'' is a subrepresentstion that is not ''V''.}}

{{glossary end}}

== Q ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=quotient}}
{{defn|1=Given a representation ''V'' and a subrepresentation <math>W \subset V</math>, the quotient representation is the representation <math>(\pi_{V/W}, V/W)</math> given by <math>\pi_{V/W}(g): V/W \to V/W, \, v + W \mapsto gv + W</math>.}}

{{term|1=quaternionic}}
{{defn|1=A [[quaternionic representation]] of a group ''G'' is a [[complex representation]] equipped with a ''G''-invariant [[quaternionic structure]].}}

{{term|1=quiver}}
{{defn|1=A [[quiver (mathematics)|quiver]], by definition, is a directed graph. But one typically studies representations of a quiver.}}

{{glossary end}}

==R==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=rational}}
{{defn|1=A representation ''V'' is [[rational representation|rational]] if each vector ''v'' in ''V'' is contained in some finite-dimensional subrepresentation (depending on ''v''.)}}

{{term|1=real}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[real representation]] of a vector space is a representation on a real vector space.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A real character is a character <math>\chi</math> of a group {{var|G}} such that <math>\chi(g)\in\mathbb{R}</math> for all {{var|g}} in {{var|G}}.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Representations and characters of groups|last=James|first=Gordon Douglas|date=2001|publisher=Cambridge University Press|others=[[Liebeck, Martin W.]]|isbn=978-0521003926|edition=2nd|location=Cambridge, UK|oclc=52220683}}</ref>}}

{{term|1=regular}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[regular representation]] of a finite group ''G'' is the induced representation of ''G'' on the [[group ring|group algebra]] over a field of ''G''.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A regular representation of a [[linear algebraic group]] ''G'' is the induced representation on the coordinate ring of ''G''. See also: [[representation on coordinate rings]].}}

{{term|1=representation}}
{{defn|no=1|{{quote box
|align=right
|width=33%
|quote=Representation theory is simple to define: it is the study of the ways in which a given group may act on vector spaces. It is almost certainly unique, however, among such clearly delineated subjects, in the breadth of its interest to mathematicians. This is not surprising: group actions are ubiquitous in 20th century mathematics, and where the object on which a group acts is not a vector space, we have learned to replace it by one that is (e.g., a cohomology group, tangent space, etc.). As a consequence, many mathematicians other than specialists in the field (or even those who think they might want to be) come in contact with the subject in various ways.
|source=Fulton, William; Harris, Joe, ''Representation Theory: A First Course''}}
A [[linear representation]] of a group ''G'' is a [[group homomorphism]] <math>\pi: G \to GL(V)</math> from ''G'' to the [[general linear group]] <math>GL(V)</math>. Depending on the group ''G'', the homomorphism <math>\pi</math> is often implicitly required to be a morphishm in a category to which ''G'' belongs; e.g., if ''G'' is a [[topological group]], then <math>\pi</math> must be continuous. The adjective “linear” is often omitted.}}
{{defn|no=2|Equivalently, a linear representation is a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] of ''G'' on a vector space ''V'' that is linear: the action <math>\sigma: G \times V \to V</math> such that for each ''g'' in ''G'', <math>\sigma_g: V \to V, v \mapsto \sigma(g, v)</math> is a linear transformation.}}
{{defn|no=3|A [[virtual representation]] is an element of the Grothendieck ring of the category of representations.}}

{{term|1=representative}}
{{defn|1=The term "[[representative function]]" is another term for a [[matrix coefficient]].}}

{{glossary end}}

==S==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Schur}}
{{defn|no=1|[[File:Schur.jpg|thumb|Issai Schur]][[Issai Schur]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Schur's lemma]] states that a ''G''-linear map between irreducible representations must be either bijective or zero.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[Schur orthogonality relations]] on a compact group says the characters of non-isomorphic irreducible representations are orthogonal to each other.}}
{{defn|no=4|1=The [[Schur functor]] <math>V \mapsto S^{\lambda}(V)</math> constructs representations such as symmetric powers or exterior powers according to a partition <math>\lambda</math>. The characters of <math>S^\lambda(V)</math> are [[Schur polynomial]]s.}}
{{defn|no=5|1=The [[Schur–Weyl duality]] computes the irreducible representations occurring in tensor powers of <math>GL(V)</math>-modules.}}
{{defn|no=6|1=A [[Schur polynomial]] is a [[symmetric function]], of a type occurring in the Weyl character formula applied to unitary groups.}}
{{defn|no=7|1=[[Schur index]].}}
{{defn|no=8|1=A [[Schur complex]].}}

{{term|1=semisimple}}
{{defn|1=A [[semisimple representation]] (also called a completely reducible representation) is a direct sum of simple representations.}}

{{term|1=simple}}
{{defn|1=Another term for "irreducible".}}

{{term|1=smooth}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[smooth representation]] of a [[locally profinite group]] ''G'' is a complex representation such that, for each ''v'' in ''V'', there is some compact open subgroup  ''K'' of ''G'' that fixes ''v''; i.e., <math>g \cdot v = v</math> for every ''g'' in ''K''.}}
{{defn|no=2|A [[smooth vector (representation theory)|smooth vector]] in a representation space of a Lie group is a vector ''v'' such that <math>g \mapsto g \cdot v</math> is a smooth function.}}

{{term|1=Specht}}
{{defn|1=[[Specht module]]}}

{{term|1=Steinberg}}
{{defn|1=[[Steinberg representation]].}}

{{term|1=subrepresentation}}
{{defn|1=A [[subrepresentation]] of a representation <math>(\pi, V)</math> of ''G'' is a vector subspace ''W'' of ''V'' such that <math>\pi(g): W \to W</math> is well-defined for each ''g'' in ''G''.}}

{{term|1=Swan}}
{{defn|1=The [[Swan representation]] is used to define the [[Swan conductor]].}}

{{term|1=symmetric}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[symmetric power of a representation]] ''V'' is a representation <math>\operatorname{Sym}^n(V)</math> with the group action induced by <math>V^{\otimes n} \to \operatorname{Sym}^n(V)</math>.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=In particular, the [[Symmetric and alternating squares|symmetric square]] of a representation ''V'' is a representation <math>\operatorname{Sym}^2(V)</math> with the group action induced by <math>V^{\otimes 2} \to \operatorname{Sym}^2(V)</math>.}}

{{term|1=system of imprimitivity}}
{{defn|1=A concept in the [[Mackey theory]]. See [[system of imprimitivity]].}}

{{glossary end}}

==T==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Tannakian duality}}
{{defn|1=The [[Tannakian duality]] is roughly an idea that a group can be recovered from all of its representations.}}

{{term|1=tempered}}
{{defn|1=[[tempered representation]]}}

{{term|1=tensor}}
{{defn|1=A [[tensor representation]] is roughly a representation obtained from tensor products (of certain representations).}}

{{term|1=tensor product}}
{{defn|1=The [[tensor product of representations]] ''V'', ''W'' is the representation that is the tensor product of vector spaces <math>V \otimes W</math> together with the linear group action <math>\pi_{V \otimes W}(g)(v \otimes w) = \pi_V(g) v \otimes \pi_W(g) w</math>.}}

{{term|1=trivial}}
{{defn|no=1|A [[trivial representation]] of a group ''G'' is a representation π such that π(''g'') is the identity for every ''g'' in ''G''.}}
{{defn|no=2|A [[trivial character]] of a group ''G'' is a character that is trivial as a representation.}}

{{glossary end}}

==U==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=uniformly bounded}}
{{defn|1=A [[uniformly bounded representation]] of a [[locally compact group]] is a representation in the algebra of bounded operators that is continuous in [[strong operator topology]] and that is such that the norm of the operator given by each group element is uniformly bounded.}}

{{term|1=unitary}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[unitary representation]] of a group ''G'' is a representation π such that π(''g'') is a [[unitary operator]] for every ''g'' in ''G''.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A [[unitarizable representation]] is a representation equivalent to a unitary representation.}}

{{glossary end}}

==V==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=Verma module}}
{{defn|1=Given a complex semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, a Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> and a choice of a [[positive Weyl chamber]], the [[Verma module]] <math>M_{\chi}</math> associated to a linear functional <math>\chi: \mathfrak{h} \to \mathbb{C}</math> is the quotient of the enveloping algebra <math>U(\mathfrak{g})</math> by the left ideal generated by <math>E_{\alpha}</math> for all positive roots <math>\alpha</math> as well as <math>H - \chi(H) 1</math> for all <math>H \in \mathfrak{h}</math>.<ref>'''Editorial note''': this is the definition in {{harv|Humphreys|1972|loc=§ 20.3.}} as well as {{harv|Gaitsgory|2005|loc=§ 1.2.}} and differs from the original by <math>\rho =</math> half the sum of the positive roots.</ref>}}
{{glossary end}}

==W==
{{glossary}}
{{term|1=weight}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The term "weight" is another name for a character.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[weight subspace]] of a representation ''V'' of a weight <math>\chi: G \to \mathbb{G}_m</math> is the subspace <math>V_{\chi} = \{ v \in V | g \cdot v = \chi(g) v \}</math> that has positive dimension.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=Similarly, for a linear functional <math>\chi: \mathfrak{h} \to \mathbb{C}</math> of a complex Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>, <math>\chi</math> is a weight of an <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>-module ''V'' if <math>V_{\chi} = \{ v \in V | H \cdot v = \chi(H)v \}</math> has positive dimension; cf. [[#highest weight]].}}
{{defn|no=4|weight lattice}}
{{defn|no=5|dominant weight: a weight \lambda is dominant if <math><\lambda, \alpha> \in \mathbb{Z}^+</math> for some <math>\alpha \in \Phi</math>}}
{{defn|no=6|fundamental dominant weight: : Given a set of simple roots <math>\Delta = \{ \alpha_1 , \alpha_2 , ... , \alpha_n \}</math>, it is a basis of <math>E</math>. <math>\alpha_1^v , \alpha_2^v , ... , \alpha_n^v \in \Phi^v</math> is a basis of <math>E</math> too; the dual basis <math>\lambda_1 , \lambda_2 , ..., \lambda_n</math> defined by <math>(\lambda_i, \alpha_j^v) = \delta_{ij}</math> , is called the fundamental dominant weights.}}
{{defn|no=7|highest weight}}

{{term|1=Weyl}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Hermann Weyl]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[Weyl character formula]] expresses the character of an irreducible representations of a complex [[semisimple Lie algebra]] in terms of highest weights.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[Weyl integration formula]] says: given a compact connected Lie group ''G'' with a maximal torus ''T'', there exists a real continuous function ''u'' on ''T'' such that for every continuous function ''f'' on ''G'', 
:<math>\int_G f(g) dg = \int_T f(t) u(t) dt.</math>
(Explicitly, <math>u</math> is 1 over the cardinality of the Weyl group times the product of <math>|e^{\alpha(t)} - e^{-\alpha(t)}|^2</math> over the roots <math>\alpha</math>.)}}

{{defn|no=4|[[Weyl module]].}}
{{defn|no=5|A [[Weyl filtration]] is a filtration of a representation of a reductive group such that the quotients are isomorphic to [[Weyl module]]s.}}

{{glossary end}}

== Y ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Young}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Alfred Young (mathematician)|Alfred Young]]}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[Young symmetrizer]] is the ''G''-linear endomorphism <math>c_{\lambda}: V^{\otimes n} \to V^{\otimes n}</math> of a tensor power of a ''G''-module ''V'' defined according to a given partition <math>\lambda</math>. By definition, the [[Schur functor]] of a representation ''V'' assigns to ''V'' the image of <math>c_{\lambda}</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

== Z ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|1=zero}}
{{defn|1=A [[zero representation]] is a zero-dimensional representation. Note: while a zero representation is a trivial representation, a trivial representation need not be zero (since “trivial” mean ''G'' acts trivially.)}}

{{glossary end}}
